    Where each of you ends up

    The full benchmark, habit by habit

    A habit scores 100 at the benchmark value and falls in a straight line to 0 at a clearly poor value (for example 5 hours of sleep, 4 hours of social media a day, or a 70-hour job). Doing better than the benchmark still scores 100, and the overall score is the plain average of the eight areas. The ideal you never does less learning than you already do; extra reading, papers and projects are added only if your week has room. If the full benchmark week does not fit into 168 hours, the model takes the shortfall from sleep, so the ideal you pays for it too.

        How the model works

        It is a structural simulation, not a curve fit. Your week drives ten linked state variables, 600 futures are simulated week by week for 260 weeks, and every comparison reuses the same random shocks so differences come from habits and not luck. The chart redraws from a fast 120-future preview and is then refined in the background.

        • Individual traits with Bayesian updating. Each simulated person draws seven traits (sleep need, energy baseline, learning rate, distraction sensitivity, burnout proneness, skill-to-pay link, memory) from a prior of 2,400 candidates. With calibration on, candidates are weighted by how well they explain your four answers and resampled, so the fan reflects people like you.
        • Sleep debt and chronic strain. Debt builds fast from every short night. Strain builds slowly from load above 50 hours and job pressure, and is paid down by days off, time off, hobbies, people and quiet time. Burnout hazard rises exponentially with strain, which is why a grind looks fine for a year and then breaks.
        • Two-store memory. Study adds to fresh knowledge, which fades with a half-life near 20 weeks unless it consolidates. Spacing, self-testing and sleep set the consolidation rate; practice and explaining set how much an hour encodes.
        • Habit feedback. Low energy brings more scrolling, fewer workouts and missed study weeks, and missed weeks make the next one likelier to be missed.
        • Fitness builds toward a level set by cardio, strength, steps and diet with diminishing returns, detrains when you stop, and feeds sleep, focus, energy, health and burnout resistance.
        • Career as a jump-diffusion. Pay drifts with skill growth, job performance and field demand; promotions and switches arrive at a rate that rises with skill, network and energy; the job market switches between expansion and downturn.
        • Unemployment and savings. A layoff starts a job search whose length depends on the market, your skill and your network. Savings drain during it, and if they run out you accept a job at about 18% lower pay.
        • Shocks. Health or family emergencies and work crunches arrive at random. The complexity setting scales their frequency and the size of all week-to-week noise.
        • Spiritual practice. Japa rounds (counting missed days), kirtan, scripture, seva and charity set a target for spiritual growth, which moves toward it slowly. Chanting time is part of your week, minus the share done during the commute or walks. Regular practice lowers strain and slightly raises energy and burnout resistance, and devotional community adds to relationships. In burnout or emergencies only part of the rounds get chanted.
        • Life index blends career, skill, health, relationships and spiritual growth with the weights you pick under Priorities.
        • Reading the chart. The bright line is the median future and the shaded bands hold the middle 50% and 80%. The curve at the right edge is the spread of outcomes in 2031, and the red strip underneath is the share of futures in burnout or without a job at each point in time.

        Limits

        • The coefficients are assumptions. They are set to plausible sizes, informed by the cited guidance where it exists, and are not fitted to a dataset. Read the direction and ranking of effects and treat exact figures as illustrative.
        • No model can predict one person's life. This one shows a range of futures under stated assumptions, and calibration narrows it only as far as four answers can.
        • It knows nothing about your employer, your field's specifics or your family, beyond generic shocks.
        • The life index weights are a value judgement. Change them under Priorities.
        • Health and fitness outputs are planning aids, not medical advice.
